title: Each leg of a rate limit is denominated in the token that actually moves, so the two legs are not comparable quantities
content:
The Fluid sUSDS ERC-4626 instance sets inflow limits of "`maxAmount`: 0, `slope`: 5,000,000 sUSDS per day" (A.6.1.1.1.2.6.1.3.1.5.1.2.4.1) and outflow limits of "`maxAmount`: 0, `slope`: 5,000,000 fsUSDS per day" (.5.1.2.4.2). The numbers match; the units do not. `sUSDS` is the supplied asset, `fsUSDS` is the vault share received.

An ERC-4626 share is worth its asset only at deployment. As the vault accrues yield the share price rises, so 5,000,000 fsUSDS becomes worth progressively more than 5,000,000 sUSDS. A symmetric-looking pair of limits therefore quietly becomes asymmetric in economic terms, in the direction of a widening outflow allowance.

The choice is forced rather than careless: a rate limit must be checked against the amount passed to the call, and `withdrawERC4626` is asset-denominated while `redeemERC4626` is share-denominated. Limits have to speak the unit of the argument they gate.

The implication for anyone reading or setting these parameters is that matched numbers do not mean matched exposure, and a limit expressed in share units silently rescales over the life of the position. Comparing inflow and outflow capacity across instances requires converting through the current share price — something no field in the Instance Configuration Document records.
description: Fluid's inflow slope is 5,000,000 sUSDS per day while its outflow slope is 5,000,000 fsUSDS per day — share units on one side, asset units on the other, drifting apart as the vault accrues yield.
